questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: A patient underwent gastrectomy for gastric adenocarcinoma. Which of the following vitamins needs to be supplemented in this patient?
questions.explanation:
A patient who has undergone gastrectomy for gastric adenocarcinoma needs to be supplemented with vitamin B12.

Vitamin B12 absorption is a complex process that relies on several factors. Intrinsic factor, a glycoprotein secreted by the parietal cells in the stomach, is essential for this process. Gastric acid and pepsin release vitamin B12 from dietary proteins, allowing it to bind with cobalophilin in the saliva. In the jejunum, cobalophilin is broken down, freeing vitamin B12 to bind with intrinsic factor. This complex is then absorbed in the distal ileum through specific receptors.  Following gastrectomy, the production of intrinsic factor is impaired due to the removal of gastric tissue, making vitamin B12 absorption difficult. Therefore, vitamin B12 supplementation is necessary after gastrectomy to prevent deficiency.

Other complications of gastrectomy include:

  • Nutritional deficiencies- Iron deficiency anemia (most common), Vitamin B12 deficiency, and osteoporosis
  • Dumping syndrome: early and late
  • Diarrhea
  • Duodenal stump leak/blow out
  • Bile reflux gastritis and esophagitis
  • Gall stones
  • Roux syndrome

questions.question: A 10-year-old child from a southern Indian state, hailing from a poor family, presents with rough and scaly skin. The child’s diet lacks vegetables and fruits. After treatment with linseed oil, Vitamin A, and Vitamin B, the symptoms subsided. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The cutaneous lesions with rough and scaly skin, with dietary history stating lack of vegetables and fruits is suggestive of phrynoderma.

Phrynoderma are keratotic follicular papules commonly present over the elbows and knees. They can also extend to the shoulders, neck, back, thighs, buttocks, and abdomen. It is also known as toad skin, due to the rough cone-shaped elevated papules. It can caused by deficiency of vitamins A, B complex, C, and E and essential fatty acids. 

When it occurs due to vitamin A deficiency, it is associated with ophthalmic symptoms like xerophthalmia, night blindness, and Bitot's spots and cutaneous symptoms like xerosis, scaling, and acne.

Management includes nutritional improvement through diet, multivitamin supplementation, and treatment of the underlying cause.

Note: Linseed oil is rich in alpha-linolenic acid, which is an essential fatty acid.

The toad skin appearance of a child with phrynoderma is given below:



Other options: 

Option A: Lichen planus is a papulosquamous lesion presenting as pruritic, purple, polygonal, planar, papules and plaques. These papules are often highlighted by white dots or lines called Wickham striae, which are created by areas of hypergranulosis. The characteristic lesions in lichen planus are shown below:



Option B: Erythroderma is a serious skin condition characterized by widespread redness (erythema) and scaling affecting more than 90% of the body's surface area. It is also known as exfoliative dermatitis and often results from underlying skin disorders, systemic diseases, or drug reactions.

Option D: Keratosis pilaris is an inherited abnormality of keratinization. It affects the follicular orifices leading to keratotic follicular plugging, perifollicular erythema, and follicular atrophy. It usually occurs during puberty. They present as small, keratotic papules on the extensor aspects of the limbs, particularly the arms which can lead to ingrowing of the hair. Treatment is purely reserved for cosmetic purposes.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question:
A patient presents to the emergency department with severe abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. The laboratory results show serum triglyceride levels > 2000 mg/dl. Which deficiency could be contributing to the patient's condition?

VLDL- very low density lipoprotein
LDL- low density lipoprotein
HDL- high density lipoprotein
questions.explanation:
The elevated triglyceride levels and symptoms of acute pancreatitis are likely related to a deficiency in apolipoprotein C II.

Apolipoprotein C2 is a lipoprotein lipase cofactor that catalyzes cleavage of chylomicrons. Defective apo C II results in type I hyperlipoproteinemia/ familial lipoprotein lipase deficiency. The resulting inactive lipoprotein lipase leads to slow clearance of chylomicrons and VLDL, and low levels of LDL and HDL. Patients present with eruptive xanthomas and acute pancreatitis.

Lipoprotein lipase is an extracellular enzyme that is present in the capillary walls of most tissues. It is chiefly synthesized by the adipose tissue, and cardiac and skeletal muscles. A deficiency of lipoprotein lipase or apo C-II leads to type 1 hyperlipoproteinemia or familial chylomicronemia which leads to an increased risk of acute pancreatitis.

Other options:

Option B: Apo B48 is involved in the assembly of chylomicrons. Defects in this protein are not associated with familial hypercholesterolemia.

Option C: Apo B100 binds low-density lipoprotein receptors. For the uptake of LDL, apo B100 acts as a ligand for the low-density lipoprotein receptor.

Option D: Apo A1 activates lecithin cholesterol acyltransferase (LCAT). LCAT is the enzyme present in HDL, which is activated by apo A1. LCAT converts free cholesterol (amphipathic) in HDL to cholesterol ester(hydrophobic). The initial discoidal shape now becomes spherical. This facilitates reverse cholesterol transport.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: After the age of 12, the boy had an intellectual disability. On examination, fingernail abrasions, excessive biting of lips, and increased levels of serum uric acid were observed. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The above clinical scenario with findings showing self-mutilation and laboratory values of hyperuricemia is most likely suggestive of Lesch-Nyhan disease.

Lesch-Nyhan syndrome is an X-linked recessive disorder due to a complete deficiency of the hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT). This deficiency results in an inability to salvage hypoxanthine or guanine leading to increased levels of phospho-ribosyl pyrophosphate (PRPP). Increased PRPP leads to increased purine synthesis, which is later degraded to uric acid. Increased hypoxanthine is also converted to uric acid.

The patients have intellectual disability, behaviors of self-injury like lip and finger biting, developmental delay, muscle dystonia, and extrapyramidal symptoms.

Diagnosis is made by the elevated levels of uric acid and by HGPRT enzyme assay.

The image given below shows the metabolism of hypoxanthine and guanine by HGPRT.



Orange diaper syndrome can be an early indicator of Lesch-Nyhan syndrome. At birth, individuals with Lesch-Nyhan syndrome typically appear asymptomatic, with normal prenatal growth and development. The condition is often first detected through the presence of orange-coloured crystals in the diaper, resulting from hyperuricemia. Since hyperuricemia is a common feature across all variants of HGPRT deficiency, which causes Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, predicting associated neurodevelopmental abnormalities requires enzyme activity testing.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: A neonate was brought with features of lethargy, and poor oral intake. On examination, a cataract was seen. Urine Benedict's test was positive but negative for Glucose. What will be the enzyme deficiency in this condition?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario of a neonate presenting with lethargy, and poor oral intake, with examination revealing a cataract and urine benedict's test was positive but negative for glucose, is suggestive of classical galactosemia and enzyme deficient is galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase.

Galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase deficiency leads to classical galactosemia. It is an autosomal recessive disorder. Normally, newborns receive up to 40% of their intake as lactose (glucose + galactose). The deficiency of this enzyme leads to an inability to convert galactose-1-phosphate to uridine diphosphate galactose. This leads to the accumulation of galactose 1-phosphate and causes injury to the kidney, liver, and brain. 

Clinical features:

  • Accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate in the liver causes liver damage & leads to hepatomegaly, vomiting, and convulsions.
  • Accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate depletes the liver of inorganic phosphate leading to diminished ATP synthesis which affects gluconeogenesis resulting in hypoglycemia.
  • Accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate in the nerves causes intellectual disability.
  • Accumulation of galactitol in the lens causes oil-drop cataracts.
  • Patients with galactosemia are at an increased risk of developing Escherichia coli neonatal sepsis.

In uridyl transferase deficiency, the epimerase is present in adequate amounts, so that the galactosemic individual can still form UDPGal from glucose. This explains how normal growth and development of affected children can occur despite the galactose-free diets.

Urinary reducing sugar (Benedict's test) and mucic acid test are positive. Direct enzyme assay using erythrocytes establishes the diagnosis.

Treatment is a galactose-free diet.



Other options:

Option A: Hexokinase is a glycolytic enzyme, involved in maintaining intracellular glucose concentration by catalysing the first step in glucose metabolism, i.e., phosphorylation of intracellular glucose.  Its deficiency leads to hemolytic anaemia. Splenomegaly may be another presenting feature. 

Option B: Galactokinase is the enzyme responsible for the conversion of galactose to galactose 1-phosphate. Only cataract is seen in the deficiency of this enzyme because galactose-1-phosphate is not formed. Hence no toxic effects of this compound are manifested. 

Option D: Phosphofructokinase is a key regulatory enzyme of glycolysis and is necessary for the ATP-dependent conversion of fructose-6-phosphate to fructose-1,6-diphosphate. Tauri's disease is type VII glycogen storage disorder that results due to the deficiency of phosphofructokinase.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: A patient diagnosed with a rare homozygous recessive condition presented with ectopia lentis. In the peripheral smear, there was no megaloblastic anemia. Later, he was found to have elevated homocysteine levels in the blood. Which of the following supplementations will help the patient?
questions.explanation:
The vitamin that can be used as supplementation in this patient with homocystinuria is pyridoxine (vitamin B6). 

Classical homocystinuria is an autosomal recessive disease most commonly caused by a deficiency of the cystathionine β-synthase. The deficiency of this enzyme leads to an accumulation of homocysteine in the blood and a clinical syndrome of intellectual disability, subluxated ocular lenses, long and slender extremities, arachnodactyly, and arterial and venous thrombi. The skeletal features of homocystinuria often mimic Marfan syndrome. Folic acid and vitamin B12 deficiency can also lead to homocystinuria with megaloblastic anemia.



Demonstration of elevated total homocysteine in the blood confirms the diagnosis. 50% of the cases of homocystinuria are termed pyridoxine-responsive because large doses of pyridoxine can enhance the activity of deficient enzymes in these patients. Administration of large doses of pyridoxine (vitamin B6) restores the activity of the deficient enzyme in half of all cases of homocystinuria.

Folate supplementation is also added to overcome any folate deficiency that might occur due to increased conversion of homocysteine to methionine. For the other 50% of the patients, the treatment consists of methionine restriction and cysteine supplementation. In addition, betaine (methyl group donor), folate and vitamin B12 may be added.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: You received a text message from your friend JOHN DOE about occupational exposure after he visited his doctor as shown below. What is the test used to diagnose?
questions.explanation:
The test for coproporphyrinogen levels is used as a screening test to diagnose lead poisoning.

Lead inhibits the enzymes delta-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) dehydratase and ferrochelatase, which are involved in heme synthesis. ALA is converted to porphobilinogen by ALA dehydratase, inhibited by lead. So, serum porphobilinogen levels are decreased in lead poisoning.

Laboratory findings include the following:

  • An elevated serum lead level
  • An elevated level of protoporphyrin in blood and elevated ALA and coproporphyrinogen in urine
  • Microcytic anemia with basophilic stippling in peripheral smear due to ineffective heme synthesis

Clinical features of chronic lead poisoning include facial pallor, anemia, basophilic stippling of red cells, blue lines in the gums, and retinal stippling. In the later phase, the findings are colic abdominal pain, constipation, nerve palsy, encephalopathy, and disturbance of the genito-urinary and cardiovascular systems.

Diagnosis of lead poisoning:

Laboratory parameter Value Remarks
Coproporphyrin in urine >150 mcg/L Screening test- indicates exposure
Aminolevulinic acid (ALA) in urine >5 mg/L Indicates lead absorption
Lead in blood >70 mcg/dL Clinical symptoms appear
Lead in urine 0.8 mg/L Indicates lead absorption
Basophilic stippling of RBCs   Sensitive indicator

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: A 3-year-old child is brought to the OPD with complaints of persistent delayed developmental milestones, and hyperpigmented macular lesions on the body which are more pronounced on exposure to sunlight. What is the error in DNA multiplication?
questions.explanation:
The history points to a diagnosis of xeroderma pigmentosum. It is characterized by defective nucleotide excision repair.

UV radiation leads to pyrimidine dimerization in DNA strands, preventing further replication by DNA polymerase. The nucleotide excision repair mechanism corrects the dimer formation in DNA. Xeroderma pigmentosum (XP) is an autosomal recessive genetic disorder characterized by an inability to repair DNA pyrimidine dimers caused by UV exposure. This leads to clinical and cellular hypersensitivity to ultraviolet (UV) radiation.

In XP the skin is normal at birth and has a three-stage progression:

  • Diffuse erythema, scaling, and freckle-like areas over the sun-exposed regions of the body at around 6 months of age.
  • The second stage is characterized by poikiloderma. This results in skin atrophy, telangiectasias with mottled hyperpigmentation, and hyperpigmentation.
  • In the third stage appearance of cutaneous malignancies like squamous cell carcinomas, malignant melanoma, basal cell carcinoma, and fibrosarcoma. 

Most of the cases with XP have ocular manifestations. Initially, it appears as photophobia, conjunctivitis, ectropion, and symblepharon with ulceration. Accumulation of pyrimidine dimer causes corneal opacification and neovascularization. Ocular malignancies are common in the lids, conjunctiva, and cornea as they are exposed to as much as facial skin. XP is ultimately fatal, and early detection of the skin lesions and their management with prevention of UV ray exposures prolong life.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question:
A patient with a family history of coronary heart disease presented with tendon xanthomas. His lipid profile showed serum LDL to be 280 mg/dL and triglyceride levels was 398 mg/dl. What is the likely defect in this patient?

LDL - Low-density lipoprotein 
VLDL - Very low-density lipoprotein
questions.explanation:
The clinical presentation with tendon xanthomas, elevated serum LDL  and elevated serum triglycerides points to a diagnosis of familial hypercholesterolemia and is due to a defect in LDL receptors.

Familial hypercholesterolemia  (type IIa hyperlipoproteinemia) is an inherited disorder due to defects in LDL receptors. This defect causes a decrease in the uptake of LDL and cholesterol. As a result, the blood levels of both LDL and cholesterol are elevated. Such patients are at increased risk of developing atherosclerosis and coronary artery disease.

Features of FH: 

  • Painful polyarthritis and tendinitis are common.
  • Physical findings seen are corneal arcus and tendon xanthomas over the Achilles tendon and the dorsum of the hands. Xanthomas are tumorous masses produced by foamy cell clusters (lipid-laden macrophages) found in the connective tissue of the skin and in tendons.

Diagnosis is done clinically based on hypercholesterolemia with 

  • LDL > 190 mg/dl, 
  • Family history of hypercholesterolemia and/or
  • Premature coronary artery disease.

Treatment includes lifestyle changes, restriction of a fatty diet, and pharmacotherapy with statins in heterozygous FH patients.

Recent drugs for specific treatment of homozygous FH are:

  • Lomitapide, a microsomal triglyceride transfer protein (MTP) inhibitor, and
  • Mipomersen, an antisense oligonucleotide against apoB.

The image below shows Achilles tendon xanthoma and a plain lateral radiograph of both ankles showing bilateral symmetrical swellings (arrows) superior to the calcaneum respectively.



Note: Lipoprotein lipase (LPL) deficiency causes type I hyperlipoproteinemia due to defects in LPL or apo C-II. Eruptive xanthomas are seen. Chylomicrons and VLDL are elevated. LDL and HDL are low. There is no risk for coronary disease.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Which food item among these is the primary source of thiamine in Indians?
questions.explanation:
Among the various food items given on the plate, the primary source of thiamine (vitamin B1) in the Indian diet is option 4 i.e. chapati and rice.

The thiamine content in various foods in decreasing order are as follows:

  • Gingelly seeds
  • Groundnut
  • Bengal gram
  • Whole wheat
  • Rice

Gingelly (sesame) seeds have the highest content of thiamine.

Thiamine is lost from rice during the process of milling. As it is a water-soluble vitamin, washing, and cooking rice cause further losses. Hence, it is advisable to avoid highly polished rice and eat parboiled or under-milled rice.

Thiamine is essential for energy metabolism, particularly in carbohydrate processing. Its active form, thiamine diphosphate, acts as a coenzyme for three critical enzyme complexes: pyruvate dehydrogenase, α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, and branched-chain keto acid dehydrogenase. This coenzyme facilitates oxidative decarboxylation by forming a reactive carbanion that attaches to carbonyl groups like those in pyruvate, leading to the release of CO2. Thiamine diphosphate is also vital for transketolase in the pentose phosphate pathway.

Thiamine triphosphate, another form of thiamin, helps regulate nerve function by activating chloride channels in nerve membranes.

A thiamine deficiency can cause several conditions such as beriberi, characterized by peripheral neuritis, which can also involve heart failure and edema. Additionally, thiamine deficiency can lead to Wernicke's encephalopathy and Korsakoff's psychosis, commonly associated with alcohol or drug abuse. The lack of thiamine impairs the conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA, leading to increased levels of lactate and pyruvate in the blood, which can result in dangerous lactic acidosis, especially in those consuming high-carbohydrate diets.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: A young female comes to the emergency department after ingesting 10 tablets of Phenobarbital. Which of the following components of the ETC is inhibited by this drug?
questions.explanation:
Phenobarbital is a barbiturate that inhibits complex I to Q of the electron transport chain. 

Complex I of the electron transport chain is NADH-Q oxidoreductase. It oxidizes NADH and reduces coenzyme Q. Phenobarbital inhibits complex I to Q so that the electrons will not be able to be transferred from NADH to coenzyme Q, which is the first step in the electron transport chain. As a result, the rate of oxygen consumption will decrease.

The electron transport chain (ETC) represents the final pathway through which electrons, originating from the oxidation of carbohydrates, fatty acids, and amino acids, are channeled toward a final reaction with oxygen to produce water and ATP. The ETC complexes are embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane.

The oxidation of compounds by ETC complexes leads to the release of free energy. This is used to pump H+ to the intermembrane space. This results in the formation of a proton motive force that is used for the phosphorylation of ADP to ATP. Thus, oxidation is coupled with phosphorylation to generate ATP. NADH generates 2.5 ATP and FADH2 generates 1.5 ATP.

The table below summarizes the inhibitors of the electron transport chain.  

Complexes of ETC Inhibitors

Complex I:

NADH-Q oxidoreductase

 Piericidin A, phenobarbital, rotenone

Complex II:

Succinate-Q reductase

 TTFA (thenoyltrifluoroacetone), carboxin, malonate

Complex III:

Q- Cyt c oxidoreductase

 BAL (British anti-lewisite), antimycin A

Complex IV:

Cyt c oxidase

 Hydrogen sulfide, carbon monoxide, cyanide 

Complex V:

ATP Synthase

 Atractyloside, oligomycin

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: A child presents to you with bone pain, hepatosplenomegaly, and pancytopenia. A trephine biopsy aspirate shows the following finding. Which of the following is the most likely enzyme deficient in this patient?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario of a child with bone pain, hepatosplenomegaly, and trephine biopsy showing Gaucher's cell with a characteristic crumpled tissue paper appearance is suggestive of Gaucher's disease. The deficient enzyme is glucocerebrosidase (also known as beta-glucosidase).

Gaucher's disease is an inborn error of metabolism caused due to a deficiency of beta-glucocerebrosidase. It is the most common lysosomal storage disorder and the mode of inheritance is autosomal recessive. There is an accumulation of lipid-laden macrophages in the spleen, liver, and other tissues.

There are three clinical subtypes - type I (chronic non-neuronopathic), type II (acute neuronopathic), and type III (intermediate). Clinical features include anemia, thrombocytopenia, hepatosplenomegaly, and neurological features depending on the subtype. 

Gaucher's cells are formed as a result of the accumulation of massive amounts of glucocerebrosides within the phagocytes. The cells have a fibrillary cytoplasm and give a crumpled tissue paper appearance.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: A 32-year-old lady comes with complaints of erythematous scaly rash, loose stools, and cognitive dysfunction. The rash involved her forearm, neck, and face. She seems to have difficulty remembering things from the recent past. Her electrolytes are within normal range. She admits to having shifted to a corn-based diet due to economic reasons. Which of the following would improve her symptoms?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical features suggests the diagnosis of pellagra, due to her corn-based diet. Oral nicotinamide supplements can improve her symtpoms. 

Niacin can be synthesized in the body from tryptophan. Two compounds, nicotinic acid and nicotinamide, have the biological activity of niacin. The nicotinamide ring of the coenzymes nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) and nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADP) participate in oxidation/reduction reactions.

The initial symptoms of pellagra include loss of appetite, generalized weakness, irritability, abdominal pain, and vomiting. This is followed by bright red glossitis and a characteristic pigmented, scaly skin rash in sun-exposed areas. This rash is known as Casal’s necklace when it forms a ring around the neck. 

The 4Ds of pellagra:

  • Diarrhea
  • Dermatitis
  • Dementia, leading to
  • Death

It is diagnosed by measuring urinary levels of 2-methyl nicotinamide and 2-pyridone.

Other options: 

Option B: Thiamine (Vitamin B1) deficiency leads to conditions like beriberi and Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, which are characterized by symptoms such as muscle weakness, peripheral neuropathy, cardiovascular issues, and confusion. While cognitive dysfunction can result from thiamine deficiency, rash and loose stools do not fit with thiamine deficiency. Therefore, thiamine would not address the full spectrum of this patient’s symptoms.

Option C: Vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy, which is associated with symptoms like bleeding gums, bruising, joint pain, and fatigue. Scurvy is not associated with a rash like the one described, nor does it typically cause cognitive dysfunction or diarrhea. Hence, high-dose vitamin C would not improve this patient’s symptoms.

Option D: Corn-based diets are low in niacin and tryptophan, leading to pellagra over time, especially if the diet is not balanced with other niacin-rich foods. While stopping the corn-based diet could prevent further niacin deficiency, it will not immediately address the existing deficiency and symptoms like rash, diarrhea, and cognitive dysfunction. The patient would still need niacin supplementation to resolve the current symptoms.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: A 3-month-old child was brought to the clinic with a history of difficulty in feeding and failure to thrive. On examination, the child is floppy, 48 cm in length and weighs 2.8 kg. There is generalized hypotonia, macroglossia and hepatomegaly. The chest x-ray of the child is given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The child with a clinical history of difficulty feeding and failure to thrive with generalised hypotonia, macroglossia, hepatomegaly and chest x-ray findings of massive cardiomegaly suggest a diagnosis of Pompe's disease.

Pompe's disease is a glycogen storage disorder(type II) caused by a deficiency of lysosomal acid maltase (alpha-glucosidase) which leads to the accumulation of glycogen in the lysosomes of the liver (hepatomegaly), skeletal muscles in the form of large vacuoles (hypotonia and weakness), cardiac muscles (hypertrophic cardiomyopathy). The child generally dies by the age of 2 years due to cardiac failure. The adult form presents with muscle dystrophies.

Laboratory findings show elevated levels of serum creatine kinase (CK), aspartate transaminase (AST), alanine transaminase (ALT), and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH). Urine glucose tetrasaccharide, a glycogen breakdown metabolite, is a reliable biomarker for disease severity and treatment response. Treatment includes enzyme replacement therapy with recombinant enzyme a-glucosidase alfa (Myozyme).

Given below is the image of muscle biopsy showing glycogen-positive vacuoles.



Other options:

Option A- Ebstein's anomaly is the teratogenic effect of maternal lithium consumption which causes a cyanotic heart disease in the newborn with atrialization of the right ventricle and conduction defects. The chest X-ray will show a box-shaped enlargement of the right atrium and pulmonary oligemia.

Option C- Transposition of great vessels is cyanotic congenital heart disease where there is a switch in the position of two main arteries i.e. pulmonary artery and aorta. X-ray shows of egg-on-string appearance with pulmonary plethora.

Option D- Von Gierke disease occurs due to a deficiency of glucose-6-phosphatase. Patients present commonly in 3-4 months of age with hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, hepatomegaly, growth retardation, hyperuricemia, and hyperlipidemia.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: A patient presented with multiple yellowish raised plaques on eyelids, xanthomas on the achilles tendon. What is the likely cause for the patient's presentation?
questions.explanation:
The clinical presentation with yellowish, raised plaques on eyelids, and tendon xanthomas points to a diagnosis of familial hypercholesterolemia (FH).

Familial hypercholesterolemia (type IIa hyperlipoproteinemia) is an inherited disorder due to defects in LDL receptors and Apo B100. This decreases the uptake of Low-density lipoprotein and cholesterol leading to their increased levels in the blood. The increased LDL accumulates in the blood vessels causing atherosclerosis (premature coronary artery disease)and in the Achilles tendon causing tendon xanthomas. Xanthomas are tumorous masses produced by foamy cell clusters (lipid-laden macrophages) found in the connective tissue of the skin and tendons. Patients can also have yellowish plaques around the eyes (Xanthelasma) and corneal arcus.

Treatment includes lifestyle changes, restriction of a fatty diet, and pharmacotherapy with statins in heterozygous FH patients.

The images below show Achilles tendon xanthoma and xanthelasma respectively:



Other options:

Option B: Tangier’s disease is a hypolipoproteinemia caused by a mutation of the ABCA1 gene. Enlarged orange tonsils are pathognomonic. Low HDL levels are seen. There is an increased risk for atherosclerosis.

The image below shows enlarged yellow-orange coloured tonsils in Tangier's disease.



Option C: Xanthomatosis is the deposition of lipids in various parts of the body like tendon xanthomas, xanthelasma, eruptive and tuberous xanthomas. This is a sign of underlying lipid metabolism disorders.

Option D: Fabry's disease is a lysosomal storage disorder with a defect in alpha-galactosidase. It causes angiokeratomas, hypohidrosis and characteristic Maltese cross deposits in urine.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question:
A child presented to the OPD with complaints of fatigue and muscle weakness while exercising. Laboratory investigations found that LCFA oxidation was affected. A muscle biopsy was done which revealed the presence of fat vacuoles. What is the probable diagnosis?

LCFA- Long-chain fatty acid

LPL- Lipoprotein lipase

LDL- Low-density lipoprotein
questions.explanation:
The clinical scenario of a child with fatigue and muscle weakness on exercise with laboratory findings of LCFA oxidation deficiency and fat vacuoles on muscle biopsy suggests a diagnosis of carnitine deficiency.

Carnitine deficiency is a defect in fatty acid oxidation that leads to hypoketotic hypoglycemia and hyperammonemia. Carnitine transports activated LCFA (long chain fatty acyl CoA) from the cytoplasm to the mitochondria for beta-oxidation (as they cannot cross the mitochondrial membrane), carnitine deficiency impairs this transport causing accumulation of lipids (skeletal muscle weakness). This excess fatty acid inhibits the urea cycle causing hyperammonemia. Since beta-oxidation cannot occur, energy production is reduced, and there is hypoglycemia without a corresponding increase in ketone bodies (hypoketotic) during times of glucose depletion such as exercise.

The role of carnitine in the metabolism of fatty acids is demonstrated in the image below:



Clinical features of carnitine deficiency begin in childhood and include poor feeding, lethargy, liver dysfunction and hepatomegaly, hypotonia, and dilated cardiomyopathy. Treatment involves oral supplementation of carnitine.

These defects result in the impaired conversion of phenylalanine to tyrosine. The patient develops clinical features due to elevated levels of phenylalanine metabolites and decreased levels of tyrosine. The excess phenylalanine in the blood is metabolized to phenylpyruvate (positive ferric chloride) and phenylacetate (mousy odour) which are excreted in the urine. Infants appear normal at birth and gradually develop symptoms of hyperreflexia, seizures, hypopigmentation, low IQ, hyperactivity, and tremors.

Patients with this condition have low serum levels of copper.

Menke's disease or Menke-Kinky hair syndrome is an X-linked recessive condition caused due to a mutation in the ATP7A gene on chromosome X. This causes impaired transport of dietary copper from the small intestine to the liver leading to low levels of copper-containing enzymes.

The final step of collagen synthesis involves the formation of covalent cross-links. This is done by the enzyme lysyl oxidase, a copper-containing protein. This is essential for the strength and rigidity of collagen. As a result of deficiency of copper in Menkes disease, this step of collagen synthesis is affected. 

The patient presents with depigmented kinky hair, failure to thrive, neurodegenerative symptoms (loss of developmental milestones, truncal hypotonia, epilepsy), multiple fractures, anaemia due to ceruloplasmin and hephaestin deficiency (converts ferrous to ferric to be bound to transferrin), neutropenia, and recurrent infections.

Option B: Zinc deficiency causes acrodermatitis enteropathica characterized by periorificial dermatitis, diarrhea, and alopecia.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: In the given Lineweaver-Burk plot, the blue line represents the action of an enzyme, and the red line represents the action of the same enzyme in the presence of an inhibitor. What is the type of inhibition shown here?
questions.explanation:
The given graph shows competitive inhibition, in which the value of Vmax remains constant and the Km value increases. The intercept on the y-axis remains unchanged while the intercept on the x-axis shifts close to zero forming a steeper slope.

Competitive inhibition is when the inhibitor binds reversibly to the substrate-binding site and competes with the substrate for the active enzyme-binding site. This effect of competitive inhibition can be overcome by increasing the substrate concentration by which maximum velocity can still be achieved. Therefore, Vmax (maximum velocity of the reaction) is unaltered in this type of inhibition. However, the concentration of the substrate required to achieve half of the maximum velocity is increased. Therefore, Km is increased in this condition.

The graph below shows the changes in Vmax and Km in competitive inhibition.



Other options:

Option B: Non-competitive inhibition is by binding inhibitors to enzymes in locations remote from the active site. Increasing the concentration of the substrate does not overcome non-competitive inhibition. Thus, noncompetitive inhibitors decrease the Vmax of the reaction. They do not interfere with the binding of the substrate to the enzyme. Thus, the enzyme shows the same Km in the presence or absence of noncompetitive inhibitors.

The graph shows the changes in Vmax and Km in non-competitive inhibition.


Option C: In uncompetitive inhibition, inhibitors bind with the enzyme-substrate intermediate complex, and inhibit it. This leads to a decrease in both Vmax and Km. An example is the inhibition of placental alkaline phosphate (ALP) by phenylalanine. 

Option D: In Allosteric inhibition, inhibitors bind to a site other than the active site i.e. allosteric site, and induce a conformational change (change in the shape of the active site unlike in non-competitive inhibition) thus, inhibiting the enzyme. ATP is an allosteric inhibitor of Phosphofructokinase in glycolysis.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Which of the following types of collagens is involved in wound healing?
questions.explanation:
Type III collagen is involved in wound healing.

Collagen types I and III predominate in the skin and aponeurotic layers. In the early stages of wound healing, type III collagen is synthesized. It is replaced by type I collagen as wound healing progresses. 

The tensile strength of the healing wound is directly proportional to the amount and type of collagen present. During healing, as disorganized collagen is degraded and reformed, covalent cross-links are formed that enhance tensile strength. The maximum strength of the healed wound depends upon the interconnection of collagen subunits. Approximately 80 percent of the original strength of the tissue is obtained by six weeks after surgery. Wounds slowly continue to get stronger but may never achieve 100 percent of their previous strength.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: In a reaction, the substrate is available in a concentration that is 1000 times the Km value of the enzyme.  After 9 minutes of reaction, 1% of substrate is converted to product (12 microgram/ml). If the concentration of the enzyme is changed to 1/3 and concentration of substrate is doubled, what is the time taken to convert the substrate into the same amount of product that i.e. 12 microgram/ml?
questions.explanation:
The time taken for the formation of the same amount of product is 27 minutes.

In this reaction, the substrate concentration becomes 1000 times i.e much greater than the Km value. Thus, the rate of this reaction is equal to Vmax and is thus independent of the substrate concentration i.e. it follows zero-order kinetics. Thus, doubling the substrate concentration does not change the velocity of the reaction i.e. it remains as Vmax.

No matter the substrate concentration, the rate of the reaction is directly proportional to the concentration of the enzyme. In this situation the enzyme concentration becomes 1/3rd. Thus, the velocity of the reaction (Vmax) also becomes 1/3rd. This means that the time taken for the formation of the same amount of product will become tripled i.e 9 × 3 = 27 minutes.

questions.question: The best method to measure HbA1C is ________
questions.explanation:
The best method to measure HBA1C is ion-exchange chromatography.

In ion-exchange chromatography:

  • Proteins interact with the stationary phase by charge-charge interactions.
  • Proteins with a net positive charge at a given pH will tightly adhere to beads with negatively charged functional groups such as carboxylates or sulfates (cation exchangers).
  • Proteins with a net negative charge adhere to beads with positively charged functional groups, typically tertiary or quaternary amines (anion exchangers).
  • Non-adherent proteins flow through the matrix and are washed away.
  • Proteins elute in inverse order of the strength of their interactions with the stationary phase.

questions.question: Which of the following does not favor euchromatin formation due to changes occurring at cytosine residues at CpG islands in DNA?

Methylation does not favour euchromatin formation due to changes cytosine residues at CpG islands in DNA.

The transcriptional regulatory regions of active genes often contain a high frequency of CpG dinucleotides (referred to as CpG islands) and they are normally unmethylated. Therefore, methylation is an epigenetic modification that inactivates DNA, and hinders the formation of euchromatin (transcriptionally active chromatin). Epigenetic changes include alterations of chromatin structure by:

  • Methylation of cytosine residues in CpG dinucleotides
  • Modification of histones by acetylation or methylation
  • Changes in higher-order chromosome structure

Sumoylation of histones (SUMO - Small Ubiquitin-related MOdifier) is associated with transcription repression. Other possible roles of posttranslationally modified histones:

  • Acetylation of core histones is associated with chromosomal assembly during DNA replication.
  • Phosphorylation of histone H1 is associated with the condensation of chromosomes during the replication cycle.
  • ADP-ribosylation of histones is associated with DNA repair.
  • Methylation of histones is correlated with activation and repression of gene transcription.
  • Acetylation of histones H3 and H4 is associated with the activation or inactivation of gene transcription.
  • Monoubiquitylation is associated with gene activation, repression, and heterochromatic gene silencing.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a true statement regarding telomerase?
questions.explanation:
The false statement is that telomerase is involved in DNA repair.

Telomeres are the end of chromosomal DNA. Since prokaryotic DNA is circular, it does not have free ends and hence no telomeres. Thus, telomeres are present only in eukaryotes  Telomeres have TG- rich repeats and usually do not code for any proteins. With every DNA replication during cell division, telomere shortening occurs. Once telomeres are almost negligible or non-existent in length, the DNA is unable to replicate and the cell dies. Hence, there is a limit to the number of times a cell can divide.

In stem cells and cancer cells, an enzyme telomerase having reverse transcriptase activity (RNA dependent DNA polymerase) adds telomeres to the chromosome ends, thereby preserving chromosomal length. It allows the stem cells and cancer cells to multiply a lot more number of times than a normal adult cell.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Gibbs free energy curve of an enzyme-catalyzed reaction is given by
questions.explanation:
Among the given graphs, the Gibbs free energy change of an enzyme-catalyzed reaction is shown by graph A (Option B).

Graph B (Option A) cannot represent the Gibbs free energy of an enzyme-catalyzed reaction, as the energy state of an intermediate cannot be lower than the product. A lower energy state of the intermediate implies that the enzyme-intermediate complex is stable and such a complex will usually not further form a product.

During any chemical reaction, the product is formed by the breaking of substrate bonds and the conformational change of the substrate into a highly unstable transition state. This transition state is denoted by the peak of the graph. The Gibbs free energy curve of an enzyme-catalyzed reaction (with no intermediate state) is shown in the image given below:



The below graph shows the normal intermediate formation with an energy state still higher than that of the product:



All the reactions have a transition state, but not all reactions have an intermediate state. Every intermediate state is again always followed by another transition state.

Activation energy is the energy difference between the free energy of the substrates and that of the transition state. Because of the high activation energy, the rates of uncatalyzed chemical reactions are often slow. 



In an enzyme-catalyzed reaction, the activation energy is reduced by forming a relatively stable intermediate-enzyme complex. Enzymes provide attachment sites for the substrate and speed up the rate of reaction. They don't change the energy state of either the substrate or the product. The Gibbs free energy change remains the same.

Graph C: Free energy change cannot be a straight line. Every reaction passes through a high-energy intermediate transition state.

Graph D: The activation energy of any reaction is never lower than the free energy of the product.

questions.question: Which of the following enzymes has the highest catalytic efficiency?

Some enzymes can be so efficient that they convert the substrate to product instantaneously. They are limited only by the rate at which substrate diffuses towards the enzyme in a solution. These are called diffusion-limited enzymes and their catalytic efficiency is as high as 108 M-1 s-1.

1. Decreased beta-oxidation of fatty acids

As the level of serum FFA is raised, proportionately more of the acetyl-CoA produced from their breakdown is converted to ketone bodies and less is oxidized via the citric acid cycle to CO2. A fall in the concentration of oxaloacetate, particularly within the mitochondria, can impair the ability of the citric acid cycle to metabolize acetyl-CoA and divert fatty acid oxidation toward ketogenesis. questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: 1. Cancer cells consume more glucose by which of the following process?
options: Increased lactate is produced even in the presence of oxygen
Increased conversion of pyruvate to acetyl CoA
questions.correct_answer: Increased lactate is produced even in the presence of oxygen
questions.explanation:
In cancer cells, increased lactate is produced even in the presence of oxygen which is known as the Warburg Effect. Neoplastic cells utilize Warburg metabolism for the generation of metabolic intermediates, which are needed for cell growth and multiplication. The Warburg Effect is a phenomenon in which there is an increase in the rate of glucose uptake and conversion into lactate(fermentation), even in the presence of oxygen. Cancer cells derive energy mainly from glycolysis.  Cancer cells utilize glycolysis (2 ATP) over mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation (36 ATP) for glucose metabolism, even though the latter produces more ATP. It is because pure oxidative phosphorylation produces abundant ATP, but also burns glucose to CO2 and H2O, leaving no carbon moieties suitable for use as building blocks for lipids or proteins. For this reason, rapidly growing cells, by undergoing glycolysis, produce carbon moieties that are needed for growth and cellular maintenance. The image given below shows the comparison of glucose metabolism in normal cells versus cancer cells.

As a result of decreased ATP production, the main metabolic function of mitochondria in growing cells is not to generate ATP, but to carry out reactions that generate cellular building blocks. For example, lipid biosynthesis. Warburg effect is produced by growth factor receptors downstream signalling pathways. These include receptor tyrosine kinase/PI3K/AKT and MYC. Clinically, cancer cells exhibiting the Warburg effect show a property of glucose hunger. This is used to visualize them via positron emission tomography (PET) scanning.

questions.question: 3. Cyanide and carbon monoxide act on which of the Heme proteins:
questions.explanation:
Cyanide and carbon monoxide act on Cytochrome c oxidase .  Carbon monoxide binds to the heme iron of cytochrome c oxidase in its reduced (ferrous, Fe²⁺) state. This prevents oxygen from binding and accepting electrons, halting the production of water and the proton gradient. Poisoning with CO can lead to severe hypoxia at the cellular level, even in the presence of normal oxygen levels. Cyanide binds irreversibly to the ferric (Fe³⁺) iron in the heme group of cytochrome c oxidase. It completely blocks electron transfer to oxygen, making it a potent inhibitor. Cyanide poisoning results in rapid cellular asphyxiation and is life-threatening.  Cytochrome c oxidase (Complex IV) in the electron transport chain (ETC) is the terminal enzyme that facilitates the transfer of electrons to molecular oxygen, reducing it to water. Various inhibitors can block this process, leading to impaired oxidative phosphorylation and ATP synthesis including hydrogen sulfide which inhibits Complex IV at high concentrations by binding to its heme groups, similar to cyanide. The zwitter bionic pH of glycine is 6. The zwitter bionic pH, also known as the isoelectric point (pI), is the pH at which an amino acid carries no net electrical charge. At this point, the molecule exists as a zwitterion - a form that has equal positive and negative charges, typically with a protonated amino group (-NH₃⁺) and a deprotonated carboxyl group (-COO⁻). For simple amino acids like glycine, which have only two ionizable groups (carboxyl and amino), the isoelectric point is calculated as the average of the two pKa values: pI = ( pK1 ​+pK2 ) / 2 ​​Given: pK1 = 2.4 (carboxyl group) pK2 = 9.8 (amino group) pI = (2.4+9.8) / 2 = 12.2/2 = 6.1, which is closest to 6 (Option A). At pH 6.1, glycine is in its zwitter bionic form and has no net charge.

questions.question: 6. How many cycles of PCR is required to generate half the copies of 26 cycles?
questions.explanation:
25 cycles of PCR is required to generate half the copies of 26 cycles.  PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction) is a method used to amplify specific DNA sequences. It involves repeated cycles of denaturation, annealing, and extension. In each cycle, the amount of DNA doubles, leading to exponential amplification. So after n cycles, the number of DNA copies is 2n .  After 26 cycles, the DNA is amplified to 226 copies. To find how many cycles are needed to produce half this amount (x),  2x = 1/2 × 226 =225  So, x = 25. Therefore, 25 cycles are required to produce half as many DNA copies as 26 cycles. PCR’s rapid and specific amplification relies on heat-stable DNA polymerases and specific primers that flank the target DNA sequence. Its applications include genetic diagnostics, forensic testing, and infectious disease detection.

questions.question: 7. A neonate was normal at birth but developed liver disease and muscle weakness 4 months later. She had severe hypoglycemia particularly in the morning after an overnight fast. On examination, there is hepatomegaly. Lab tests done after fasting show ketoacidosis, pH 7.25, increased ALT and AST levels. On administering IV glucagon after a carbohydrate meal, a normal rise in blood glucose levels is seen whereas on giving IV glucagon after an overnight fast, no rise on blood glucose levels is seen. Liver biopsy shows increased glycogen (8% of weight). Which enzyme has a defect?
questions.explanation:
The clinical vignette is suggestive of Cori's disease which has a defect of debranching enzyme. A key diagnostic clue is the liver biopsy showing increased glycogen content (8% of liver weight), indicating that glycogen is being stored but not effectively broken down. Importantly, the IV glucagon test showed a rise in blood glucose after a carbohydrate meal, but no rise after an overnight fast - this suggests that glycogen is present in the liver but cannot be fully mobilized during fasting. Glycogen debranching enzyme deficiency (glycogen storage disease III) is also known as Cori's disease, Forbes' disease, and limit dextrinosis. The debranching enzyme, together with phosphorylase, is responsible for the complete degradation of glycogen. In this case, the debranching enzyme is defective; hence, the glycogen breakdown is incomplete, which results in the accumulation of abnormal glycogen with short outer-branch chains, which resemble limit dextrin. Cori’s disease can present with fasting hypoglycemia, hepatomegaly, hyperlipidemia, and growth retardation. Muscle weakness is slowly progressive and associated with wasting. Accumulation of limit dextrins is seen in Cori's disease. Definitive diagnosis is through enzyme assays in the liver, muscle, or both. The purpose of the glucagon challenge test is to help differentiate types of glycogen storage diseases (GSDs), particularly Von Gierke’s disease (Type I) and Cori’s disease (Type III). When glucagon is given after a carbohydrate meal, a normal rise in blood glucose occurs in Cori’s disease, because some glycogen is still accessible for breakdown. However, after prolonged fasting, glucagon does not raise blood glucose in either Von Gierke's or Cori’s disease. In Von Gierke’s, glucose-6-phosphatase is defective, so no glucose is released at all, even after feeding.

Muscle glycogen is abnormally high and blood lactate is low after exercise. It does not cause hypoglycemia or liver enlargement, so it doesn't fit this case. Option C: Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency (Von Gierke disease) causes severe fasting hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, and ketosis. There is no glucose rise even after a meal, unlike in this patient. questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: 9. Gene pool refers to all the alleles in ________
questions.explanation:
Gene pool refers to all the alleles in population.  Gene pool is defined as the total genetic information present in all the breeding individuals of that population. This concept is central to sexually reproducing species, where individuals interbreed and share genetic material. The gene pool changes over time due to mutations, natural selection, genetic drift, and gene flow between populations. It reflects the overall genetic diversity and evolutionary potential of a population.

questions.question: 10. A 4 year old child presents with developmental regression, hepatomegaly, and a cherry-red spot in the macula. The startle reflex is normal. Which of the following lysosomal enzymes is deficient?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario of developmental regression along with hepatomegaly, macular cherry-red spot, and normal startle reflex point to a diagnosis of Niemann-Pick disease. The enzyme deficient in this disease is sphingomyelinase. Niemann-Pick disease presents in infancy and usually leads to death by 2-3 years of age. The affected infants are normal at birth, but deteriorate rapidly with failure to thrive. The usual clinical presentation includes hepatosplenomegaly and rapid psychomotor retardation. Niemann-Pick disease occurs due to the deficient activity of acid sphingomyelinase enzyme. There is an extensive accumulation of sphingomyelin in the monocyte-macrophage system. Lipid-laden foam cells are observed in bone marrow and lymph nodes. The diagnosis is confirmed by measuring the sphingomyelinase levels in the peripheral leucocytes.  This condition is managed with supportive treatment, such as physical therapy and a feeding tube for nutrition. Olipudase alfa has been recently approved for non-CNS manifestations of Niemann-Pick disease.  Other options: Option B: Hexosaminidase A deficiency is seen in Tay-Sachs disease. While it also presents with progressive neurodegeneration and macular cherry-red spot, there is no organomegaly and lysosomes with onion skin are seen. Startle reflex is exaggerated in Tay-Sachs disease.  Option C: Glucocerebrosidase deficiency is seen in Gaucher disease. The patients present with hematological abnormalities, organomegaly, and skeletal manifestations in the form of bone pain and pathological fractures. Bone marrow examination shows macrophages with a characteristic crumbled tissue paper appearance. Option D: Arylsulfatase A deficiency is seen in Metachromatic leukodystrophy. It primarily causes demyelination and psychological disturbances, and does not present with hepatomegaly or a cherry-red macula. questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question:
Which is the correct sequence of steps in the isolation of desirable protein using recombinant DNA technology?
  1. Expression of protein and lysis of bacterial cell
  2. Incorporation of genes into bacteria
  3. SDS PAGE
  4. Protein elution  
  5. Hybridization
questions.explanation:
The correct sequence of isolation of desirable protein in recombinant DNA technology is 2, 1, 3, 5, 4.

I) Incorporation of genes into bacteria: The gene needed to produce the desired proteins is to be incorporated into the bacteria. This is done using cloning vectors like bacterial plasmids, phages, or cosmids. The DNA of interest is ligated into the vector DNA and is called recombinant DNA. This vector is then inserted into a competent host cell (eg: E.coli bacteria) where it is replicated.

II) Expression of protein and lysis of bacterial cell:  After incorporation of recombinant DNA, bacteria express the inserted gene and produce the desired protein on a large scale along with other indigenous bacterial proteins. To release these proteins bacterial cell is lysed.

III) SDS-PAGE (sodium dodecyl sulfate-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis): It is the most widely used method for determining the purity of a protein. After the proteins are released, to separate the desirable protein, we subject it to SDS-PAGE. It separates proteins based on molecular weight.

IV) Hybridization and blotting: It is done to confirm that the isolated protein is the desired protein. It is done using western blotting techniques on nitrocellulose paper.

V) Protein elution - extraction of the produced protein.

 

The practical applications of recombinant DNA technology include:

  • Gene mapping using techniques such as fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH).
  • Producing proteins such as:
    • Interferons, tPA (tissue plasminogen activator)
    • Insulin, growth hormone
    • Hepatitis B vaccine
  • Molecular analysis of disease, to detect gene variations and mutations.
  • Restriction Fragment Length polymorphism (RFLP) and single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP)
  • Microsatellite DNA polymorphisms
  • Gene therapy and bone marrow transplantation

questions.question: Which of the following techniques is used to detect DNA-protein interaction?
questions.explanation:
The technique used to detect DNA-protein interaction is DNA footprinting.

The parts of DNA that are protein-bound (Eg: RNA polymerase bound to the promoter region of DNA) are resistant to digestion by nuclease enzymes. Since the nucleases are unable to cleave the protein-bound regions of DNA, when the cleaved DNA fragments are run on polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis, there are missing bands indicating, protected sites of protein-bound DNA. These missing areas represent the footprint of the protected DNA-protein complexes. Hence DNA footprinting technique helps to identify the specific binding site of protein on a DNA sequence.

The image below illustrates the DNA footprinting technique.



Other options:

Option B: DNA fingerprinting uses RFLPs (restriction fragment length polymorphism) or repeat sequence DNA to identify a person's unique pattern of DNA. Polymorphisms are inherited differences found among individuals. with this technique, individuals can be differentiated by variations in their DNA sequence, using restriction endonucleases followed by gel electrophoresis, to visualize RFLPs. DNA fingerprinting is used for forensic analysis of crime scenes, and for paternity testing. 

Option C: ELISA uses antibodies linked to certain enzymes to detect certain antigens present in the sample.

Option D: Northern blotting technique can be used to detect RNA. Here, the mixture of mRNA molecules is separated by electrophoresis and then transferred to a nitrocellulose membrane and hybridized with radiolabeled probes.

questions.question: A patient was diagnosed with Ewing sarcoma with EWSR1 gene mutation. The technique shown in the image was performed to confirm the diagnosis. Identify the technique shown in the image.
questions.explanation:
The technique shown in the image is FISH demonstrating a positive EWSR1 gene rearrangement, characteristic of Ewing sarcoma. The fused region denoted by Yellow corresponds to a normal intact gene, while a split signal pattern showing separate red and green signals is indicative of EWSR1 gene rearrangement.

Fluorescent In Situ Hybridisation (FISH) is a simple technique for the detection of specific genetic information on morphologically intact tissue using fluorescent probes. FISH can be performed on prenatal samples, peripheral blood cells, touch preparations from cancer biopsies, and even fixed archival tissue sections. It is used to detect

  • numeric abnormalities of chromosomes (aneuploidy)
  • subtle microdeletions and rearrangements.
  • complex translocations that are not demonstrable by routine karyotyping
  • gene amplification (e.g., HER2 in breast cancer or NMYC amplification in neuroblastomas)

Other options:

Option B: Karyotyping is the process by which chromosomes are isolated, stained, and examined to find chromosomal anomalies. It is used in prenatal diagnosis, investigation of repeat pregnancy loss, investigation of children and adults suspected of having a chromosomal disorder, and subtyping of lymphomas and leukemias for the purpose of exact diagnosis, giving a prognosis, and treatment.

Option C: IHC (Immunohistochemistry) is a staining method for histopathological specimens. It helps in the diagnosis and classification of tumors based on their distinct protein expression patterns. Eg: The expression of estrogen receptor (ER), progesterone receptor (PR), and HER2/neu in breast cancer cells is mainly assessed by immunohistochemistry.

Option D: Sanger's technique: This was the first technique used to determine the sequence of proteins. The first protein to be sequenced by this method was insulin. Sanger’s reagent is 1- Flouro 2,4 Dinitro benzene. Only dipeptides and tripeptides can be sequenced by this method.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: In a patient with maple syrup urine disease, all of the following amino acids should be restricted in diet except?
questions.explanation:
In maple syrup urine disease (MSUD), only branched-chain amino acids are restricted, hence, methionine does not need any restriction in diet.

Branched-chain amino acids are:

  • Leucine (L)
  • Isoleucine (I)
  • Valine (V)

MSUD is an autosomal recessive disorder in which there is a partial or complete deficiency of branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase complex (BCKD). This impairs the metabolism of branched-chain amino acids. These amino acids, particularly leucine and their metabolite accumulate in the blood, causing toxic effects on the brain. Features include feeding problems, vomiting, ketosis, and a characteristic burnt sugar odor /maple syrup-like odor found in urine, sweat, and cerumen.



Laboratory investigations will show increased levels of branched-chain amino acids in the plasma and urine. Leucine levels are usually higher than isoleucine, and valine.

Treatment involves restricted intake of branched-chain amino acids using commercially available formulas and judicious supplementation of isoleucine and valine. Very high levels of leucine are removed by hemodialysis.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Which of the following statements about the human genome project is false?
questions.explanation:
The human genome project did not use next-generation sequencing.

The Human Genome Project (HGP) was an international, collaborative research program, which involved agencies such as UNESCO, HUGO, the National Institute of Health/Department of Energy (USA), the Medical Research Council (UK), Genethon (France), and the European Union. The primary goal of the Human Genome Project was to determine the sequence of all nucleotide base pairs, that make up human DNA and to create a single linear map of all genes from the human genome. The project was active from 1990 to 2003, taking around 13 years to complete. A total of 20500 genes were identified and mapped. Scientists used various methods of first-generation sequencing technologies including sanger's technique, SGS technique, etc. The HGP has produced a curated and accurate reference sequence for the majority of human chromosomes. The reference sequence has provided the foundation for the use of second-generation sequencing technologies such as array techniques.

Next-generation sequencing (NGS) is a new technology used for sequencing DNA and RNA and mutation detection. NGS can sequence the genome faster and in a shorter period of time than first-generation sequencing technologies. NGS allows for the detection of a spectrum of mutations, including single nucleotide substitutions, small insertions and deletions, large genomic duplications and deletions, and rare variations. Next-generation DNA sequencing technologies include

  • Illumina sequencing
  • Roche 454 sequencing
  • Ion torrent: Proton/PGM sequencing
  • SOLID sequencing.

The banding technique used for dicentric chromosomes is C banding.

Heterochromatin includes non-coding regions of DNA, such as centromeric regions. The staining of these constitutive heterochromatins, is done by C-banding using silver salt staining. A dicentric chromosome having two centromeres can hence be identified by C banding.

Various techniques are used in karyotyping to study chromosomes. Staining with various compounds produces various results and helps us to understand the chromosomes better.

  • G banding - Giemsa staining after partial denaturation of chromatin. It is the most common technique used in cytogenetics to produce a visible karyotype by staining condensed chromosomes.
  • R banding - Reverse Giemsa staining. In this, the light and dark areas are reversed.
  • C banding - staining of heterochromatin with silver salts.
  • T banding - staining the telomeres of chromosomes.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Affinity maturation of antibodies is because of?
questions.explanation:
Affinity maturation of antibodies is because of somatic hypermutation.

Affinity maturation is the process by which antibodies gain increased affinity, avidity, and anti-pathogen activity. It is a result of somatic hypermutation of immunoglobulin genes in B cells, coupled with selection for antigen binding.

Somatic hypermutation is a cellular response by which the immune system adapts to the new foreign elements that confront it. They do so by adding nucleotides in V gene regions of heavy and light chains, resulting in a better fit of antigen with the antibodies. This hence increases the affinity of antibodies to antigens. Due to this, the subset of plasma cells with these improved hypervariable regions are more strongly
selected by the antigen and therefore constitute a larger part of the population of antibody-producing cells. This process is called affinity maturation.

This process occurs in the germinal centers and proceeds for weeks after acute infection or vaccination, or for many cycles during chronic infection. The resulting antibodies can be highly mutated from their germline-encoded counterparts, with an increase in several orders of magnitude in affinity for antigen compared to the corresponding naïve B cell receptors (BCRs).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Best method for detection of mutations with low allele frequency is
questions.explanation:
Best method for detection of mutation with low allele frequency is Droplet digital PCR (ddPCR)

It is an advanced and more precise type of quantitative PCR which gives more consistent and reproducible results. It can accurately quantify the target nucleic acid sequence within a sample. It is useful for determining somatic mutation with low allele frequency. Mutant alleles of frequency as low as 0.25% can also be detected using this technique. 

Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) is a rapid automated method for the amplification of specific DNA sequences (or genes). Reverse transcriptase PCR- The enzyme reverse transcriptase (RT) is used to synthesize a complimentary copy of DNA (cDNA) from RNA and this cDNA is then used as a template for PCR.

Other special PCR types:

Nested PCR- It involves the sequential use of two primer sets. The first primer set is used for amplification and the target sequence for the second primer is present only on the amplicon with the target sequence. Nested PCR is intended to reduce non-specific binding due to the amplification of unexpected primer binding sites.



Multiplex PCR- Multiple primers are used to amplify several DNA sequences simultaneously. As this process targets multiple genes at once, a single test run gives additional information that would otherwise require several times the reagents and technician time to perform. 

The Sanger sequencing technique is used for DNA sequencing. It is based on controlled termination of synthesis of DNA by using chain terminating agents like dideoxynucleotides.

Fluorescent In Situ Hybridisation (FISH) is a simple technique for the detection of specific genetic information on morphologically intact tissue using fluorescent probes. FISH can be performed on prenatal samples, peripheral blood cells, touch preparations from cancer biopsies, and even fixed archival tissue sections.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: In Sanger sequencing, ddNTP is used because:
options: It is used to increase DNA polymerase activity
They exhibit higher affinity for DNA polymerases
It doesn't allow further elongation of DNA
questions.correct_answer: It doesn't allow further elongation of DNA
questions.explanation:
In Sanger sequencing, dideoxynucleotides triphosphates (ddNTP) are used because it doesn't allow further elongation of DNA.

The Sanger method is used for DNA sequencing. This method uses the mechanism of synthesis of DNA by DNA polymerases. In the process of synthesis of DNA, the 3'-hydroxyl group of primer reacts with an incoming dNTP to form a new phosphodiester bond. This reaction is catalyzed by DNA polymerase.

In the Sanger sequencing method, ddNTP is used because it halts the DNA synthesis. ddNTPs can bind to the template strand but lack the 3'-hydroxyl group which is required to add the next nucleotide. The products of this reaction are a mixture of DNA strands of varying lengths. This mixture is then separated using polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis and autoradiography. This produces a pattern of bands from which the DNA sequence can be read.

The image given below shows the steps involved in Sanger's method. 



 

Sanger’s technique was the first technique used to determine the sequence of proteins. The first protein to be sequenced by this method was insulin. Sanger’s reagent is 1- fluoro 2,4 dinitro benzene.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Misincorporation of uracil into DNA is seen in deficiency of:
questions.explanation:
Misincorporation of uracil into DNA is seen in the deficiency of folate. 

Folate deficiency leads to decreased thymidylate synthesis from deoxyuridylate due to deficient methylation of deoxyuridine monophosphate (dUMP) to thymidine monophosphate (TMP). The methylation of dUMP to TMP is catalyzed by thymidylate synthase and requires tetrahydrofolate (THFA) as a methyl group donor. This decreased TMP synthesis can result in an imbalance of deoxyribonucleotides and hence leading to excessive uracil misincorporation into DNA during replication and repair.

Folic acid (vitamin B9) is a water-soluble vitamin, and its active form is tetrahydrofolate (THFA). It acts as a carrier of one-carbon groups. Tetrahydrofolate receives one-carbon fragments from donors such as serine, glycine, and histidine and transfers them to intermediates in the synthesis of amino acids, purines, and pyrimidines.

 


Folate deficiency results in:

  • Megaloblastic anemia 
  • Homocystenemia
  • Neural tube defects (spina bifida, Anencephaly) in the fetus.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Deamination of methylated cytosine forms which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Deamination of methylated cytosine forms thymine.

Deamination is the removal of an amino group(NH2) from a chemical compound. Enzymes that catalyze this reaction are called deaminases. Deamination of 5-methylcytosine forms thymine. 

Other significant deaminations are given below:

  • Deamination of adenosine forms inosine. This is a metabolic step involved in uric acid formation by purine catabolism. It is mediated by the enzyme adenosine deaminase (ADA). ADA deficiency leads to sparse or defective T cells and B cells and patients suffer from Severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID).
  • Deamination of cytosine leads to uracil formation - The production of apolipoprotein B-48 (apoB-48) in the intestine is the result of RNA editing in the intestine. This involves post-transcriptional deamination of cytosine to uracil by enzyme cytidine deaminase. This converts sense codon (CAA) in the mRNA to nonsense codon (UAA)at a single specific site. This edited mRNA translates to apoB-48.
  • Deamination of guanine forms xanthine. This is a metabolic step involved in uric acid formation by purine catabolism.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Which of the following types of inhibition is depicted in the given Lineweaver-Burk plot?
questions.explanation:
The given graph shows competitive inhibition, in which the value of Vmax remains constant and the Km value increases.

  • Km is the substrate concentration at which velocity is half maximum.
  • Vmax is the maximum velocity of a reaction.
Inhibition Km Vmax
Competitive Increases Same
Non Competitive Same Decreases
Uncompetitive Decreases Decreases

 

Competitive inhibition is when the inhibitor binds reversibly to the substrate-binding site and competes with the substrate for the active enzyme-binding site. This effect of competitive inhibition can be overcome by increasing the substrate concentration by which maximum velocity can still be achieved. Therefore, Vmax is unaltered in this type of inhibition. However, the concentration of the substrate required to achieve half of the maximum velocity is increased. Therefore, Km is increased in this condition.

The graph shows the changes in Vmax and Km in competitive inhibition.



Other options:

Option B: Non-competitive inhibition is by binding inhibitors to enzymes in locations remote from the active site. Increasing the concentration of the substrate does not overcome non-competitive inhibition. Thus, noncompetitive inhibitors decrease the Vmax of the reaction. They do not interfere with the binding of the substrate to the enzyme. Thus, the enzyme shows the same Km in the presence or absence of noncompetitive inhibitors.

The graph shows the changes in Vmax and Km in non-competitive inhibition.


Option C: In uncompetitive inhibition, inhibitors bind with the enzyme-substrate intermediate complex, and inhibit it. This leads to decrease in both Vmax and Km. An example is the inhibition of placental alkaline phosphate (ALP) by phenylalanine. 

Option D: Suicidal inhibition is a special type of irreversible inhibition. The inhibitor here makes use of the enzyme's own reaction mechanism to inactivate it and is hence known as mechanism-based inactivation. An example is allopurinol, which is oxidized by xanthine oxidase to alloxanthine. Alloxanthine in turn is a more potent inhibitor of xanthine oxidase.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Glycogen phosphorylase is activated by:
questions.explanation:
Glycogen phosphorylase is activated by calcium in the muscle.

Glycogen phosphorylase is the rate-limiting enzyme of glycogenolysis and is decreased in the fed state.

In the muscle, the increased cytosolic calcium ion concentration initiates both contraction and glycogenolysis. Muscle phosphorylase kinase has four different subunits, α, β, γ, and δ. The α and β subunits are phosphorylated by cAMP-dependent protein kinase. The δ subunit is identical to the calcium-binding protein calmodulin and binds four calcium ions. Calcium coordinates the activation of Glycogen Phosphorylase with the contraction of the muscle.

Glycogen phosphorylase catalyzes the cleavage of α1 → 4 linkages of glycogen to single units of glucose 1-phosphate. It uses pyridoxal phosphate as the coenzyme. Different isoenzymes of glycogen phosphorylase are seen in the liver, muscles, and brain.

Other options:

Option B: During glycogenolysis, glucose 6-phosphate allosterically inhibits glycogen phosphorylase. 

Option C: Insulin entirely suppresses glycogenolysis in the skeletal muscle and liver.

Option D: In glycogenolysis protein phosphatase is inactivated by inhibitor proteins in response to cAMP, to maintain the glycogen phosphorylase in an active state.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Mutation of the gene of cystic fibrosis occurs with:
questions.explanation:
The mutant gene of cystic fibrosis (CF gene) produces a mutant CFTR protein with the deletion of a phenylalanine residue at 508 (F508del), characterised by impaired chloride secretion.

Cystic fibrosis is a condition with an autosomal recessive mode of inheritance. It results due to a defective mutation in the gene encoding for cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CF gene). It plays an important role in mucociliary transport along the respiratory mucosa. It also helps to regulate the amount of exocrine gland secretion.

The defect in the ion channel results in the production of hyper-viscous, adherent secretions which can obstruct the airways. Organisms such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus can grow in the sputum. The exocrine pancreas can undergo fibrotic scarring, cyst formation, and acinar tissue loss. The viscid secretions can lead to pancreatic duct obstruction. The flow of digestive enzymes to the duodenum is hence impaired.

Symptoms include sinusitis, steatorrhea, and abdominal pain. Distal intestinal obstruction is a complication due to difficulty in excreting intestinal contents. In neonates, it can present as meconium ileus. 

Detection of high levels of trypsinogen is used in newborn screening. Chloride level >60mEq/L in the sweat of affected patients is diagnostic. Hyponatremic hypochloremic alkalosis is seen.

Postural drainage, short-term antibiotics, and inhaled bronchodilators can be used for medical management. The definitive treatment is lung transplantation.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: A baby is brought to the OPD with complaints of lethargy and poor feeding. On examination, it is noted that the urine had a smell of burnt sugar. A defect in which of the following enzymes causes this disease?
questions.explanation:
The diagnosis, in this case, is that of maple syrup urine disease (MSUD). This disease occurs due to a defect of the enzyme branched-chain keto acid dehydrogenase.

 MSUD is an autosomal recessive disorder that occurs due to a deficiency of branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase complex. This impairs the metabolism of branched-chain amino acids valine, leucine, isoleucine, and alloisoleucine. These amino acids, particularly leucine and its metabolite accumulate in the blood, causing toxic effects on the brain.

The affected child develops poor feeding and vomiting a few days after birth. There is a period of hypertonicity with a period of flaccidity in between. These appear as repetitive boxing and bicycling movements. The babies may also have hypoglycemia, but this is not corrected by the administration of glucose. The urine, sweat, and cerumen of the baby have a sweetish maple syrup-like odor.

Laboratory investigations will show increased levels of branched-chain amino acids in the plasma and urine. Leucine levels are usually higher than isoleucine, valine, and alloisoleucine. Since the patient excretes ketone bodies in the urine, the urine will be positive for the dinitrophenylhydrazine test.

Treatment involves controlled intake of branched-chain amino acids using commercially available formulas and judicious supplementation of isoleucine and valine. Very high levels of leucine are removed by hemodialysis.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: All are true about the hexose monophosphate shunt, except:
questions.explanation:
The hexose monophosphate (HMP) shunt produces ribose and does not utilize it. 

The pentose phosphate pathway, also known as the HMP shunt pathway, is an alternative route for the metabolism of glucose. It contributes in two major ways:

  • Formation of NADPH for the synthesis of fatty acids and steroids and maintenance of reduced glutathione for antioxidant activity.
  • Formation of ribose for the synthesis of nucleic acid and nucleotides

The enzymes for this pathway are found in the cytosol. There are two phases:

  1. Irreversible oxidative phase: Glucose-6-phosphate is dehydrogenated and decarboxylated to form ribulose-5-phosphate which in turn gets converted to ribose-5-phosphate.
  2. Reversible non-oxidative phase: Ribulose-5-phosphate is converted back to glucose-6-phosphate.
